item.title: Youtube Channels Inspiration List (Work In Progress): Youtube Channels Inspiration List (Work In Progress)
item.content:encoded:
There are a great number of Youtube channels that produce content that can be really useful and inspirational when you work on SCPs and tales. I've collected quite a few myself over the years, so I thought it would be useful to make a list of Youtube channels that can help us write.

What I really want is contributions. I'm going to start the list, but I want to expand it as much as possible. I'm going to use a format that will make it as fast as possible for people to find what they're looking for. If you contribute, please use the following format:

1. Include a link to the channel (preferably the channel main page, not just a video from the channel).
2. The name of the channel.
3. The category that they channel fits in (see categories below, might add more as time goes).
4. Description of the content on the channel. Try to include a little bit about who might be interested in the channel. See below for a framework.

Also note: The channel has to be somewhat directly relevant to writing SCPs. SCPs focus on phenomena that deviate from the norm. The list shouldn't include channels that delve into more mundane topics, even if those topics might be relevant to a story. It might be useful to research how a diesel engine works if you're writing a SCP focused on that topic, but it's not going to be even remotely useful to most people who write SCPs.

+ show block
– hide block

Youtube Channels

General Writing / Storytelling

Diana Callahan - Quotidian Writer
Link
Diana Callahan is focused exclusively on writing, with an emphasis on story, plot, dialogue and character.
Who is this for? Diana Callahan is a very well-rounded channel about writing that can probably teach every aspiring writer something.

Just Write
Link
Just Write focuses on looking at popular works of fiction, primarily movies, and trying to decipher what good lessons can be learnt from the work to improve your own writing.
Who is this for? Anyone who wants to use popular works of fiction as a foundation to improve their own writing.

Lessons from the Screenplay
Link
Lessons from the Screenplay, obviously, focuses on screenplays, often focusing each video on a single movie, going over the screenplay to explain what makes it so effective. Has a lot of videos that focus greatly on dialogue.
Who is this for? Anyone looking to cinema for tips on how to build tension and write beautiful dialogue.

SCP specific content

The Exploring Series
Link
To many on these forums, The Exploring Series was the gateway drug to the rest of the SCP community. Each video goes over a single SCP, telling the tale of the SCP in an interesting and captivating way, combining the story with images appropriate to it.
Who is this for? Everyone, but especially people who are yet not that familiar with the SCP foundation.

Real life - Investigation and policework

JCS - Criminal Psychology
Link
JSC focuses on the psychology of criminals, using interrogation videos as his primary source of information.
Who is this for? This channel is an invaluable asset if you want to create realistic interrogation scenes in your writing.

Real Life - Psychology

Dr. Todd Grande
Link
Dr. Todd Grande focuses on making psychological profiles of real-life murders and serial killers. Some of his profiles focus on other interesting people who are somehow outliers of society.
Who is this for? Anyone looking to create much more realistic and grounded characters, especially evil or malevolent characters.

Real Life - Philosophy

Academy of Ideas
Link
A channel that goes into great detail on some of the darker writers in philosophy and psychology. The channel explores archetypes, shadow projection, despair and similar topics.
Who is this for? Anyone who wants to learn more about the darker philosophers like Carl Jung, Nietzsche and Kirkegaard.

Real Life - Mysteries and peculiar phenomena

Lemmino
Link
Channel that focuses primarily on real life mysteries, like the Bermuda Triangle or Dyatlov Pass Incident.
Who is this for? Anyone looking to find information on the real life mysteries that often inspired SCPs.

Fiction - Horror

Acolytes of Horror
Link
Acolytes of Horror specializes in making fewer, but fairly long and in-depth analyses of horror. Primarily he analyses movies, but some of his videos focus on the historic influences on modern-day horror.
Who is this for? Anyone looking to really delve deep into the psychology and symbolism of effective horror.

The Vile Eye
Link
The Vile Eye makes psychological profiles of famous evil characters, from Nurse Ratchet in One Flew Over The Cuckoo's Nest, to Michael Meyers from Halloween.
Who is this for? Anyone who wants to create a memorable evil character.

Ryan Hollinger
Link
Ryan Hollinger makes videos where he analyzes various horror movies, discussing what makes them effective.
Who is this for? Anyone looking to widen their background knowledge on horror movies.

Fiction - Thriller and Drama

Fiction - Science Fiction

DUST
Link
Amazing channel that produces high-quality short sci-fi movies, each with stories that could easily have been fitted inside the SCP universe.
Who is this for? This is one of the few channels here that I would recommend for everyone, but in particular anyone interested in the short sci-fi format.

Isaac Arthur
Link
This channel focuses on hard sci-fi topics such as Dyson Spheres and Matrioshka Brains as well as hypothesizes about aliens. A lot of the material might be a bit too large in scale to fit into the SCP universe.
Who is this for? Anyone who's interested in hard sci-fi and civilizations on a galactic scale.

John Michael Godier
Link
The creator of this channel is a science-fiction writer who focuses on hard sci-fi, with an emphasis on realism. The content describes a lot of hypothetical science fiction phenomena.
Who is this for? Anyone who's interested in hard sci-fi, especially concepts such as multiple universes and alien civilizations.

Like Stories of Old
Link
This channel is very philosophical, it goes into deep detail on topics such as time travel, the hero's journey, global pandemics and empathy. It can help create an emotional and philosophical underpinning to any story you tell.
Who is this for? Anyone who wants to learn more about how sci-fi concepts and story tropes connect to a deeper philosophical and psychological truth.

Quinn's Ideas
Link
Quinn's Ideas focuses very heavily on the Dune universe, and as such goes into tremendous detail on topics such as psychic powers, genetics and omniscience. If you haven't read the Dune books, there are videos several hours long that go through each book. Has lately also started making videos on H.P. Lovecraft.
Who is this for? Anyone who wants to learn more about the Dune universe without reading all of the books. Also a great source of inspiration if you're writing on omniscience and related psychic powers.

Fiction - Urban Legends and Creepypasta

Dark5
Link
A short-form channel where various urban legends and creepypasta are vividly explained with accompanying images.
Who is this for? Mainly for those interested in the creepypasta format.

Top 5 Scary Videos
Link
Top 5 videos discussing monsters and scary stories taken from both fiction and urban legends. Features creations from several of our SCP contributors.

Audiobooks

HorrorBabble
Link
Has all of the H.P. Lovecraft books, as well as many other horror writers such as Robert Bloch

As a courtesy to our mobile users, please collapse long forum posts. ~ McB

item.title: Memetic, Cognitohazard or Infohazard?: Memetic, Cognitohazard or Infohazard?
item.content:encoded:
Strangely enough, I dreamt up an SCP that I'd like to put on paper. But I'm not sure what kind of threat it would be considered.

Here's the gist: Just viewing the anomaly (Let's call it SCP1) won't do anything. It's when you feel fear towards it that it will be triggered. Oddly enough, there is another SCP (Let's call it SCP2) that essentially resets your thoughts on a subconscious level and overrides your fear towards SCP1, slowing it down.

There is a potential to reverse and neutralize SCP1 altogether if enough people around the world view SCP2. Hence, SCP2 would probably be classified as Thaumiel.

But the more pertinent question is what kind of hazard would SCP1 be?

Any help is greatly appreciated!

item.title: Anyone here familiar with Dissociative Disorders?: Re: Anyone here familiar with Dissociative Disorders?
item.content:encoded:
Hi Tyyronious,

I can't offer any personal advice on DID specifically, but rather some suggestions on how to find the information you need.

This site & forum will have thousands of people very familiar with SCP and a tiny number familiar with DID (or other types of multiplicity) — that's not what you need, you aren't after SCP-specific information, you need a broad range of DID experience.

A better option might be to try a mental health support forum with a media/off-topic discussion section, where you'll find a far higher number of people who know far more about DID, many of who will be very aware of its depiction in various media. It dosn't matter that they won't know anything about SCP, since you just need to talk about writing fiction in general, and not going into detail about SCP could help reduce potential conflict/misunderstanding.

The movie "Split" from a few years ago is perhaps a good reference point — read up on the mental health community's criticism of that movie. Find a MH forum with a suitable discussion section and post on there what you're doing in a general sense, discuss the problems of Split (and other films / books / TV), talk about your personal experiences of DID, and say that you want to ensure that what you write is representative of DID in general rather than just your own experience.

item.title: Translating C++ Syntax to Real Life: Re: Translating C++ Syntax to Real Life
item.content:encoded:
Hi DeathByGin (what a civilised way to go!),

Obviously the whole "magic is computer programming" trope is very well established, so you can take advantage of much of that for starters. But as you start to go into more depth and more specificity I think the first thing to consider is why C++ in particular — if there's a certain reason then that may well tie strongly into how you want to do it.

As for the language itself, is it inherently anomalous, or is there something else that makes it anomalous. Could it be, for example, that it's just regular C++ until you include a library that changes what can be done

 #include <adamic>

once included the library allows the code to manipulate the fabric of the universe.

Then I'd suggest considering how the code is being run — is it compiled before being run (in which case is the language itself inherently anomalous, or does compiling turn it into something Skippy)? Does the house itself run the code (on what's inside it), or is the code being run by some(thing/one) else on the house (and what's within), or just on the things inside the house (the house isn't involved at all other than just being where the cleaning occurs), can it clean outside the house, can it clean other houses, etc? These sort of things likely determine whether or not the house is a variable

In the end I think my suggestion would likely be to use pseudocode in a C++ style

Lastly, going back to the "magic is computer programming" trope… I'm now imagining a host of angelic computer programmers spending their time porting the universe from Fortan/Cobol into C++, everything that's weird/wrong in the universe is a consequence of all the usual problems that huge software projects have…

item.title: Dactylic structure for English: Re: Dactylic structure for English
item.content:encoded:
I'm very unfamiliar with the usage of dactylic hexameter in English. Longfellow's Evangeline appears to have been written in it, but that's one of the few examples that I could find that actually was. I'm also unsure what the exact rules for syllable length in English are, since I know that they're different from both Latin and Greek. Looking at Evangeline is probably your best lead.

I do have to say that if your goal is to write an Iliad-like poem in English, I wouldn't actually worry about keeping dactylic hexameter. Very few translations of the Iliad keep the meter intact in any form, and something using the meter would actually feel stiff and somewhat fake. I'd recommend choosing a new form of meter more familiar to an English reader, which would capture the sense and feel of dactylic hexameter without actually being it. Accurately using dactylic isn't something I would do unless you were planning to do composition in Ancient Greek, and even then I would still use a different meter for an English translation.

item.title: Need help with a broadcasted SCP: Re: Need help with a broadcasted SCP
item.content:encoded:
The range of a radio broadcast depends on a number of factors, so lets start with the basics…

Radio is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, so in theory has unlimited range (radio astronomy studies objects billions of ly away). But… the signal strength diminishes with range - the further it travels, the more is spreads out, the weaker it gets. The signals can also be absorbed or reflected by things they encounter.

+ show block
– hide block
There are two main ways of encoding information on a radio signal - amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM)

AM encodes information by varying the strength (height) of the signal, while FM varies the frequency (squashing & stretching). Nowadays AM is pretty dead, FM still dominates, with DAB is becoming increasingly common (steadily replacing FM in most places)

Different frequencies can also behave differently - shortwave, UHF, etc. Notably shortwave can be bounced of part of the atmosphere called the ionosphere to give a range of thousands of miles

So…

Generally speaking, numbers stations were shortwave - so unless it's highly directional & line-of-site probably dosn't make sense given the short range you're talking about.

On the other hand, the range does suggest it's line-of-site — so it will depend on the height of the antennae and distance to the horizon.

My suggestion might be using FM and broadcasting in the VHF range. FMs big advantage is quality - it's much less susceptible to interference than AM.

If you want it feeling old-fashioned (eg something from the cold war) then shortwave would make sense - but it would be vulnerable to over-the-horizon reception by bouncing off the ionosphere, which you'd either need to allow for or do something specific to mitigate. Long range, non-directional, non-los was after all the whole point for them!

Researchers are to keep any broadcast recordings on a remote data server (I don't know if that's even possible with radio recordings)

Absolutely - the nature of the recordings dosn't matter, once they're captured locally just transfer them from the local computers to the remote storage (specifics obviously vary depending on how they're networked).

Remember - it dosn't have to be DAB to be recorded, there's no fundamental reason you can't record broadcast you just need an extra step or two (eg the computer needs some sort of connection to an FM receiver)

Researchers are able to communicate with the entity making the broadcast using a HAM Radio set to the same frequency as the station (I have no clue if HAM Radios work that way. Would I need to change the station to HAM Radio?)

Ham radio operators were obsessive about numbers stations, so you may want to consider making that a factor in how your scip was discovered. Ham radio transmission is restricted to specific frequency bands over a range of (LF to VHF) frequencies, the specific ranges are mostly standardised but vary a bit in VHF, and vary a lot in certain countries (hazard a guess which one!)

But, there's no particular reason why SCP would have to stick to the approved Ham frequencies if they're only transmitting in a certain area (so their broadcasts don't interfere with anyone else). Similarly there's no particular reason (other than cost & convenience) why they'd specifically use Ham equipment rather than either general radio equipment or something custom

item.title: Ergospheres and Black Hole Stuff: Re: Ergospheres and Black Hole Stuff
item.content:encoded:
Hi Ryze,

A few thoughts based in part on half-remembered astrophysics lectures…

What would happen if a ship maintained orbit around a spinning supermassive black hole?

In general, if you're far enough out (outside any accretion disc) and pick the right orbit there's no reason to think it wouldn't just go round and round and round and round. BH don't magically "suck" things in, their gravity is just as strong as anything else with the same mass, and indeed if they formed from the death of a single star their mass will be less than that of the original star.

You probably want to avoid accretion discs — the ring of matter (gas, dust, planets, stars, etc) spiralling into the BH. Probably best if there's no accretion disc at all, but you almost certainly don't want to be orbiting within it - risk of collisions, plus your orbit probably either won't be stable so you'll need additional station keeping, or will be constrained by magnetic fields.

Infalling matter means there will be bursts of radiation from time to time — high energy electromagnetic burps whenever the BH swallows an asteroid from its accretion disc. This will be most pronounced at the poles (orthogonal to the plane of the accretion disc) where anything risks getting frazzled by such a burst

+ show block
– hide block

Two things you mention are worth pointing out, don't really affect the answers but you may want to keep them in mind…

spinning

It's expected that all natural astrophysical black holes rotate - although there are solutions for non-rotating ones they aren't expected to occur naturally because whatever they formed from would have some amount of angular momentum that would be preserved during collapse

If a BH wasn't rotating then that would be a strong indicator of something weird

supermassive

SMBH are *big*, they're the things in the centers of galaxies, generally a minimum of 1 million solar masses and going up to billions (the Milky Way's is believed to be around 4M). BH in general are a bit weird, and SMBH are (in some ways) differently weird, for example…
- the radius of a BH scales linearly with mass, and the volume of a sphere scales with the cube of the radius… so as the mass (and size) of a BH goes up the density falls… you've heard that Saturn could float in a sufficiently large pool of water, yes? So could a sufficiently large SMBH
- related to that, you know the idea of people getting stretched out as they cross a BH event horizon… that's because of the gravitational gradient - gravity is getting much stronger over a short distance, so gravity is a lot stronger at your feet than it is at your head… but with a SMBH that effect is diminished, you could cross the event horizon without even noticing the gravitational gradient until you were a long way inside!

What if somebody was to broadcast a message in the ergosphere?

The ergosphere is the region of space close to a rotating BH that gets dragged around as the BH spins, a bit like water gets swirled around by something rotating in it. Much like signals are "bent" by gravity around any high mass, so will they be "dragged" around in the ergosphere. note that the ergosphere depends on the rotation, so extends furthest along the plane of rotation and disappears at the poles.

You're going to run into problems with both directionality and degradation that I'd expect to cause huge problems for any general purpose inter-spaceship communication system, but which could probably be mitigated by having specifically designed systems and the receiving ship in a particular location relative to the sending ship. Indeed, I think (not sure) that sending/receiving would be significantly easier/harder depending on relative position - so you may want the ship outside the ergosphere to change position depending on whether its sending or receiving (maybe, really not sure)

What if something faster than light flew towards a black hole?

As Reimann said - whatever you want!

Our understanding of how BH behave is based (in part) on General Relativity, GR assumes Special Relativity, which assumes a finite & limiting speed of light. In particular — anything that has a mass cannot travel at the speed of light, anything that dosn't have a mass must travel at the speed of light, nothing can be accelerated from less than c up to c, etc.

So how they interact is entirely up to you, there isn't a "right" answer — pick what you want to achieve and hand-wave the specifics

For example, you might consider that there is a v>c event horizon, it's just smaller than the normal v=c one so a superluminal particle could get inside the normal event horizon, as long as it dosn't get too far inside. Of course then you need to consider what's "inside" the EH, which is perhaps the far more complicated part!

what are professional terms surrounding these things

A few things to consider and/or read up on…

No Hair theorem
BH are all practically identical, they have no distinguishing physical qualities, and are entirely described by just three quantities

  • all naturally occurring BH will rotate & will therefore have angular momentum
  • they have charge - but it will almost always be neutral or very close to neutral
  • other than those two they just have their mass (mass-energy)

This is known as the "no hair theorem", and is generally believed to be true

Penrose process
You can (in theory) "mine" energy from the ergosphere by exploiting conservation of angular momentum to reduce the angular momentum of the BH while increasing the kinetic energy of an object in the ergosphere. The usual description of this considers a rocket entering the ergosphere (jettisoning mass over the EH in such a way as to reduce the AM, then gaining KE to conserve momentum) or an orbiting space station with a tether lowered into the appropriate region of the ergosphere

Information paradox
Quantum mechanics really dislikes the idea that information (in general, and specifically about a wave function) can be destroyed, so what happens to the information associated with a particle when it falls into a BH? The "no hair" theorem says that there's no way for that information to be preserved (by encoding it within the BH). This was the subject of much debate (and a few funny bets) between some big-name physicists. The current assumptions tend to be along the lines of the information is preserved by being encoded in quantum fluctuations on the event horizon and subsequently contained in Hawking radiation (see also the Holographic Principle for more on encoding a description of an object on its boundary)

how would you theoretically destroy one?

As Riemann mentioned, they evaporate through Hawking radiation — you'll just need to wait a few billion years for it to happen!

You could remove mass-energy somehow, but "simply" feeding it anti-matter wouldn't work as that has the same mass-energy as normal matter. Maybe that's where you could use the ftl particles you mentioned - perhaps although they couldn't be used to extract information they could be used in a similar way to the Penrose process, only rather than reducing angular momentum they reduce mass-energy

Or you could add angular momentum - spinning the BH faster could (in theory) cause the event horizon to disappear. Specifically, I think, the event horizon only exists if M^4 > J^2 (I think). Then the question is… what's left behind when the event horizon is gone?

Hope that's helpful (and, possibly, even right!)
